prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of work, in prose above all and rooted in poetry, that builds a metaphysical architecture out of memory, the body and dream.

statement.case_for: My choice of B043 is unchanged, and I base it on the common criteria, not on how colleagues ordered the candidates. The voice is the test I care most about: it should be audible in the writing and nowhere else on the list. As publicly described, Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid build recursive worlds from childhood memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation in long, syntactically ambitious prose. The project looks like one sustained undertaking whose parts extend each other. The chair asked what would show this beyond the two best-known titles. From public knowledge, the earlier prose such as Nostalgia and Travesti, the long poem Levantul and the early lyric collections suggest a comic, grotesque and parodic register alongside the visionary one. That answers part of the breadth objection, because the oeuvre is not a single solemn mode. I have not read these in the original and cannot verify them, so I offer this as a pointer for the committee's reading, not as established fact. The attribution is clean, with one writer and one language. After the exchange I have changed the citation wording but not the laureate. I no longer name poetry as a co-equal pillar, and I drop lineage claims and 'lifetime's work' phrasing. Poetry stays as the root of the prose, which is what the thinner translated coverage can support.
statement.case_against: The case still depends on sentence rhythm, syntactic density and register in Romanian, which I can judge only through translation and critical accounts. Digressive maximalism may be excess rather than depth in some long books, and quality across the corpus may be uneven. I would lower B043 if committee readers found that the later novels mainly repeat the motifs of the early trilogy, or if the comic and historical registers prove thin on the page. I would also lower it if the translated poetry showed nothing the prose does not already do. The poetry and early work are thinner in translation, so any whole-oeuvre claim is partly an inference. If the committee judged that inwardness limits significance more than I now think, Adonis or Michon would become the more secure choice on specific criteria. For Adonis that criterion is a long formal project in a language with a deep tradition. For Michon it is concentrated, unmistakable prose.

responses.point: Olsson moved from placing Carson first to placing Cărtărescu first. He keeps Carson as his first alternative on formal radicalism, and he reads her translations and scholarship as part of one sustained engagement with antiquity, not only as a complication.
responses.response: Olsson's distinction is useful, and it is a better argument than the genre objection. If the translations and scholarship feed the original work, they bear on the whole-oeuvre judgment. Whether they belong in the citation is a separate question, because a citation has to rest on literary work the committee can read as text. I did not rank Carson in my own list, and I hold that loosely, since my knowledge of her work is narrower than for the other candidates. I do not claim a settled verdict on her. I am persuaded that the weight of her case falls on a few landmark books, and he names this himself as the reason for his revision. I would not exclude her for being hybrid. I would ask whether a developing arc beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox can be shown from the texts.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Cărtărescu first but asks whether the inward, maximalist mode limits the breadth of his significance. She keeps Adonis as her first alternative, and she says she cannot judge his prosody as directly as a novelist's structures.
responses.response: I take the breadth question as the real test of my own choice. Part of my answer is the range of registers in the oeuvre. The comic, grotesque, bodily, historical and speculative material should be argued from the texts, and I have named the volumes I would send the committee to. The remaining part is that significance should not be measured by outward subject matter alone. An inward project can have wide significance if the form renews what the novel can hold. She says this is where Cărtărescu's strength lies, and I agree. I also agree with her caution about Adonis. A limited ability to assess his Arabic is a limit on the assessor, not a verdict on him. That is why I keep him as an alternative and not a lead.

responses.point: Palm separates sustained ambition from sustained quality in Cărtărescu's density, and she ranks Michon third because small volume and the difficulty of translating his French make significance across the whole oeuvre hard to establish.
responses.response: I accept the separation between ambition and quality, and it should shape what the committee reads. It cannot be settled by reputation. I would ask readers to compare a late novel with an early one on whether the formal problem changes, not whether the themes persist. On Michon we agree on the facts and differ slightly in weight. I think a small, concentrated body of work can be a complete achievement, which is why I ranked him second and keep him as an alternative. I also agree that his effect lies in syntax and register, which are the features translation loses most. For that reason I would not make him the lead unless the committee reads him in French.

responses.point: Carlberg asks whether Palm's lower ranking of Adonis reflects the poetry itself or the limits of translation. She says the same limit applies to every language-bound candidate, including Cărtărescu, and should not be applied selectively.
responses.response: I agree with the principle, and I will apply it to myself. I read Cărtărescu through translation too. My confidence in him therefore rests on structure, scale and voice, which survive translation better than rhythm does. It does not rest on a claim about his Romanian sentence. For both writers the committee should say plainly what it can and cannot judge, and ideally hear from readers of Romanian and Arabic. I see no principled reason to discount one language-bound poet and trust another. My preference for B043 comes from the criteria of sustained quality and breadth, and I do not think that relies on a double standard. It does mean I should not treat Adonis's unverifiable features as a weakness in him.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and proposes a citation of a visionary prose 'rooted in Romanian poetry' across 'a lifetime's work'. He also lists the gap in translated poetry as a limit on how much weight poetry can carry.
responses.response: I agree that the gap in the poetry limits the citation. It is why I narrowed my wording to prose rooted in poetry. I would go one step further than his draft. 'Across a lifetime's work' and any claim of lineage, such as being rooted in Romanian poetry or European modernism, assert more than the evidence in front of us can support, as the chair's summary notes. A concise citation should claim only what the committee can defend from the texts it has read. I would keep the lyric root as a modest, defensible phrase and drop the rest.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic achievement survives translation, and whether quality is sustained throughout the long, digressive books. The chair's question about which later volumes show this is not fully answered by public knowledge.
Whether the comic, grotesque and historical registers I point to are as substantial on the page as public descriptions suggest. I have not read the original texts or independently verified them.
Whether the poetry and early prose, thinner in translation, support the 'rooted in poetry' wording in the citation.

Whether Carson's original literary work is large and developing enough to carry a whole-oeuvre citation. My own knowledge of her work is narrower than for the other candidates, and not ranking her was not a considered verdict.
Whether Michon's small corpus and Adonis's Arabic prosody can be judged adequately in translation, and whether the committee has original-language readers for Romanian, French or Arabic.
All judgments rest on general public knowledge and translated or reported evidence. I have not verified sources and I make no claim about actual nominations or proceedings.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, professional or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist and critic of historical and psychological fiction is context, not evidence of a preference.
